As the Russian-Ukrainian war, which long ago entered a phase of attrition, grinds on, Russia, Ukraine and the United States began a new round of US-brokered trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on November 10. The talks are scheduled to continue on November 11.
The talks follow a successful humanitarian operation in Oleshky, a southern Ukrainian town that has been occupied by Russian forces since 2022.
Starting in December 2025, Oleshky experienced a food crisis that worsened dramatically in the summer of this year. Over the years under Russian occupation, its population declined from 25,000 to 2,000 people, and the food crisis threatened the survival of those who remained. In the summer, however, Ukrainian and Russian intelligence services agreed to work on a local ceasefire in order to evacuate Oleshky’s inhabitants – if they wanted to leave – either to Ukraine or to Russia.
The humanitarian mission went surprisingly smoothly. Both sides stood by the ceasefire agreement, hundreds of people were successfully evacuated (mostly to Ukraine) from the long-suffering town, and it was extraordinary to see the Ukrainian and Russian human rights representatives, Dmytro Lubinets and Yana Lantratova, coordinating the humanitarian mission peacefully and with mutual respect.

Islamabad, Pakistan – In the spring of 2025, Pakistan and India severed most of their remaining links after years of acrimony.
Gunmen had killed 26 people in Pahalgam in India-administered Kashmir that April. New Delhi blamed Pakistan for the attack – Islamabad denied any role – and put the Indus Waters Treaty, governing the sharing of rivers flowing into Pakistan, in abeyance. Pakistan retaliated by closing its airspace to Indian airlines, shutting the Wagah border crossing and suspending trade.

Container ships are seen at a port in Lianyungang, Jiangsu province, China, on November 10, 2026 [CN-STR/AFP]By John PowerPublished On 11 Nov 202611 Nov 2026
China’s $1.04 trillion trade surplus in the first 10 months of the year is a testament to its mighty export engine.
It is also a sign of structural weaknesses that, left unchecked, threaten to derail China’s bid to join the ranks of the wealthiest nations.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Massive fire as Israeli settlers burn down business near Nabluslist 2 of 4Fire contained on platform in Iran’s South Pars gas fieldlist 3 of 4‘Everything and everyone we love is at stake’: Thunberg slams COP31 talkslist 4 of 4Spain holds state funeral for 69 victims of deadly train crashend of list
While its status as the world’s factory helped it achieve a dramatic rise in living standards beginning in the late 1970s, China’s export-led economic model is facing diminishing returns.
Even as the AI boom drives its exports to record highs, the world’s second-largest economy suffers from chronically weak domestic demand.
Chinese consumers save far more than their peers elsewhere, with households typically putting away one-third or more of earnings.
The dynamic can be partly explained by China’s relatively weak social safety net, as well as cultural attitudes, an undervalued currency and a flailing real estate market.
China spends far less on social protection than most advanced economies.
Government spending on healthcare, pensions and welfare payments accounts for only about 10 percent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), far below the OECD average of about 23 percent.
With more money stowed away for a rainy day, Chinese households also spend less.

US Vice President JD Vance, shakes hands with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Prime Minister's Office on October 22, 2025 in Jerusalem, Israel [Nathan Howard/Pool/Getty Images]
When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu eventually leaves office – and he may be on his way out sooner rather than later, following last month’s general election – he will leave behind a long record of damage inflicted on his country and its people, as well as on others.
Strategically, however, one of his most damaging legacies, particularly for the security and wellbeing of the Jewish state, will be the rapid deterioration of its relations with its closest and most consequential ally, the United States. This is not simply a falling-out with America’s political elite; relations with the American public have also suffered.
Worse still, replacing Netanyahu may not be enough to halt the erosion of relations between the two countries, with potentially serious consequences for Israel’s security, economy and international standing. A change of government might, at best, salvage some of what has been lost.
US President Donald Trump’s announcement, on the day of the US midterm elections, that the United States would phase out approximately $4bn in annual military aid to Israel by the end of 2026 came as a surprise, primarily because of its timing and the prospect that decades of assistance would come to such an abrupt end.
It may have been a last-ditch attempt to avert a landslide Congressional victory for the Democrats, but the decision to gradually phase out the aid had reportedly been agreed some time earlier.

By Hanna Duggal and Marium AliPublished On 11 Nov 202611 Nov 2026
Hackers have twice taken control of supermarket fridges across Europe in less than a month, sparking fires and spoiling millions of euros’ worth of food.
On October 11 and 12, attackers heated units at about 700 French stores to as high as 50C (122F). On November 2, a second wave of suspected cyberattacks affected supermarkets and food businesses in at least nine European countries, including Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden.Empty freezers at a Paris supermarket after the October 2026 cyberattack on French stores’ refrigeration systems. The sign reads: ‘Our store has been hacked, and our refrigeration system has been affected.’ [Lucien Libert/Reuters]
France has since blamed the first attack on Shahid Kaveh, a cyberunit affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), calling it the first large-scale sabotage cyberattack on French soil. It is not yet clear who was behind the second wave.
The attacks have raised concern about how exposed internet-connected equipment has become, from industrial machinery to household appliances. Al Jazeera illustrates the devices at risk in your home and the essential services you rely on, and what you can do to protect yourself.
How can a fridge be hacked?
A supermarket’s fridges and freezers are run from one control panel, which is connected to the internet so contractors can manage it remotely. Home smart fridges connect the same way, through Wi-Fi, an app or a cloud service.
